text: After the last two lessons, the mechanics of both tools are clear. The harder, more useful skill is recognizing which one a given requirement actually calls for, and that comes down to a single question: does this rule only need to hold true on the form, or does it need to hold true no matter how the record is written? If the answer is just the form, you're improving the form experience, and a UI Policy is the right tool. If the answer is no matter how it's written, you're protecting data integrity, and a Data Policy is the right tool.

A UI Policy alone is the correct, sufficient choice whenever the goal is pure user-experience convenience, with no real consequence if some other write path happens to bypass it. Hiding a field that's irrelevant to the current record, purely to reduce visual clutter, is the textbook case — nothing breaks if an import or an API sets that field anyway on a record where it doesn't matter. A UI Policy that makes a field read-only just to stop a user from fat-fingering a value nobody else is realistically going to touch is the same kind of low-stakes, UX-only call.

A Data Policy is the right call the moment a rule is actually a data-integrity requirement, something that must be true of the record itself, independent of who or what created it. Business Justification being mandatory for any Priority 1 Incident, even if that incident arrived through an API integration with a ticketing tool, is exactly this shape. The business doesn't care whether a human filled out a form or software posted JSON — it cares that no Priority 1 incident exists anywhere without a justification, and only server-side enforcement can make that guarantee.

In real practice, many administrators lean on a simple working default: reach for a Data Policy any time there's a genuine data-integrity requirement, and reserve UI Policy for pure form convenience with no integrity stakes attached. That default holds up well because a Data Policy can still mirror its behavior onto the form through Apply to UI, so choosing it rarely costs you the live feedback a UI Policy would have given anyway. The one thing you lose by defaulting to Data Policy is visibility control — hiding or revealing a field can only ever come from an actual UI Policy.

In practice, plenty of real-world requirements end up using both tools together: a UI Policy to hide and reveal fields for a clean, uncluttered form, plus a Data Policy to guarantee the mandatory and read-only rules hold everywhere else. Next up: Business Rules — a mechanism with none of these boundaries at all, which makes it both far more powerful and far riskier than anything covered so far.
